Anak
ā'nak
n. (the father of a race of giants in the hill country about Hebron, whose sons made ten of the twelve spies despair)
From Hebrew 'Anaq, connected with a word for a neck-chain or collar — long-necked, and so tall. His descendants are the Anakim, the sons of Anak.

Biblical Definition

Anak is the ancestor of the tall men who held the hill country around Hebron when the twelve spies went up. The report names them: “they ascended by the south, and came unto Hebron; where Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the children of Anak, were” (Num 13:22). Ten of the spies made the sight of them the argument against faith — the people be strong, the cities walled and very great, “and moreover we saw the children of Anak there” (Num 13:28) — and then went further: “there we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants: and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight” (Num 13:33). That last sentence is the anatomy of unbelief. They measured themselves against the giants, decided what they looked like in another man's eyes, and never once put God into the comparison. Caleb did the arithmetic differently and never forgot it; forty-five years later, an old man, he asked for that very hill: give me this mountain, for the Anakims are there, “if so be the LORD will be with me, then I shall be able to drive them out” (Jos 14:12). And he did: “Caleb drove thence the three sons of Anak” (Jos 15:14) — the same three, named again, taken by the one man who had believed the LORD when the giants were only a rumour.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Anak; in sacred history he is the father of the Anakim, a race of giants dwelling about Hebron in the land of Canaan.

expand to see more

ANAK, n. The father of the Anakim, a race of tall men in the south of Canaan.

His sons Ahiman, Sheshai and Talmai dwelt at Hebron, called also Kirjath-arba.

The spies sent by Moses reported that they saw the children of Anak there.

The name is thought to signify long-necked, and so of great stature.

Caleb drove out the three sons of Anak when Hebron was given him for an inheritance.

Key Scripture

Num 13:22 — "And they ascended by the south, and came unto Hebron; where Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the children of Anak, were. (Now Hebron was built seven years before Zoan in Egypt.)"

Num 13:28 — "Nevertheless the people be strong that dwell in the land, and the cities are walled, and very great: and moreover we saw the children of Anak there."

Num 13:33 — "And there we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants: and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight."

Jos 15:14 — "And Caleb drove thence the three sons of Anak, Sheshai, and Ahiman, and Talmai, the children of Anak."

Modern Corruption

The Anakim are either dissolved into folklore or inflated into a mythology of fallen-angel hybrids; and the spies' unbelief is softened into understandable caution rather than named as the sin that killed a generation.

expand to see more

Two speculative excesses attend this text. The first treats the giants as legend, a folk memory dressed up to explain ruined walls. The second builds an elaborate mythology on the word rendered giants, linking the Anakim to the Nephilim of Genesis 6 and constructing a system of angelic-human hybrids surviving the flood. The dictionary keeps to what is written. Moses reports tall, formidable men in the hill country of Canaan; Deuteronomy compares their stature to the Emims and the Zamzummims; and the point of the passage is not their genetics but Israel's faith. Where Scripture is silent, speculation should be silent too — and a doctrine built on the fringes of Genesis 6 has left the ground of the plain word.

The second corruption is a pastoral one. The ten spies gave a report that was factually accurate in nearly every particular; their sin was not bad data but a comparison with God left out of it. Hebrews names the failure precisely: “they could not enter in because of unbelief” (Heb 3:19) — not because of the giants. Modern Christians are urged to be realistic about obstacles and are seldom warned that realism which never reaches as far as the promises of God is the very thing that killed a generation in the wilderness. Caleb saw the same walls and the same men. He simply added the LORD to the sum, and lived to take the mountain.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'Anaq (H6061), Anak; 'Anaqim, the sons of Anak; nephilim (H5303), giants, fallen ones; chagab (H2284), grasshopper; Chebron (H2275), Hebron.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'Anaq (H6061) — Anak; father of the Anakim, associated with a neck-chain, so long-necked.

Hebrew nephilim (H5303) — the word rendered “giants” in Num 13:33.

Hebrew chagab (H2284) — grasshopper, locust; the spies' estimate of themselves.

Hebrew Chebron (H2275) — Hebron; their stronghold, and Caleb's inheritance.

Hebrew yarash (H3423) — to possess, dispossess, drive out; Caleb's word for what he meant to do.

Usage

"“We saw the children of Anak there” — accurate reconnaissance, and no faith in it."

"“We were in our own sight as grasshoppers” — unbelief measuring itself against the wrong thing."

"“Caleb drove thence the three sons of Anak” — forty-five years later, the same three, by name."
